Selby
SEL-bee
n. (the Yorkshire Benedictine abbey founded about 1069, whose church survives whole as a parish church)
From Old Norse selja, a willow, with by, a settlement; the willow village on the Ouse.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Selby Abbey stands on the Ouse below York, founded about 1069 by a monk named Benedict from Auxerre who claimed a vision directing him to a place marked by three swans, and endowed by William the Conqueror, who was then in Yorkshire burning it. It was the first Benedictine house founded in the north after the Conquest, grew rich on the Ouse trade, and its abbot was one of only two in the north to be mitred. At the Dissolution the monastery was suppressed and the great church, unusually, was kept; it was bought for the parish, survived a fire in 1906 that gutted it, and was rebuilt. Its Norman nave and the east window remain. The dictionary records Selby for its founding story, which turns on a vow. Benedict vowed to build where the vision sent him and did it, and monastic life was constructed entirely on vows of that kind, which is the point at which Scripture has something severe to say. A vow is not a devotional ornament; it is a debt, and the warning is that it is better not to vow at all than to vow and not pay.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a vow as a solemn promise made to God; to pay as to discharge a debt; to defer as to put off; to slack as to be remiss; and to require as to demand as of right.

expand to see more

VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God, or by a pagan to his deity; a promise by which one binds himself to an act, service or condition.

PAY, v.t. To discharge a debt; to deliver to a creditor the value of what is due to him; to fulfil, as a promise.

DEFER, v.t. To delay; to put off; to postpone to a future time; to procrastinate.

SLACK, a. Not tense; not hard drawn; remiss; not holding fast; weak; not earnest or eager.

REQUIRE, v.t. To demand; to ask as of right and by authority; to claim as by right; to exact.

Key Scripture

Ecc 5:4 — "When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed."

Ecc 5:5 — "Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay."

Deu 23:21 — "When thou shalt vow a vow unto the LORD thy God, thou shalt not slack to pay it: for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee; and it would be sin in thee."

Psa 76:11 — "Vow, and pay unto the LORD your God: let all that be round about him bring presents unto him that ought to be feared."

Modern Corruption

Yorkshire Benedictine abbey founded about 1069 on the strength of a monk's vision and vow, whose church survived the Dissolution as a parish church.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the seriousness of a vow, which Scripture treats as a contracted debt rather than a pious gesture. The Preacher gives the command and the reason together: “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools” (Ecc 5:4), and then the safer counsel for anyone inclined to promise freely, “Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay” (Ecc 5:5).

The live temptation in monastic religion was to multiply vows and then to administer them, dispensing, commuting and selling relief from obligations men had taken on themselves. The law allows no such machinery: “When thou shalt vow a vow unto the LORD thy God, thou shalt not slack to pay it: for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee” (Deu 23:21). Where vows are made rightly they belong with worship and not with bargaining: “Vow, and pay unto the LORD your God” (Psa 76:11). Selby's founder paid his; the system built on such promises did not keep them so well.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew neder (H5088), a vow; Hebrew shalam (H7999), to pay or complete; Hebrew achar (H0309), to delay; Hebrew darash (H1875), to require.

expand to see more

Hebrew neder (H5088) — a vow, a votive promise; “When thou vowest a vow unto God”, Ecclesiastes 5:4.

Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to complete, to pay; “pay that which thou hast vowed”, Ecclesiastes 5:4.

Hebrew achar (H0309) — to delay, to tarry; “defer not to pay it”, Ecclesiastes 5:4.

Hebrew darash (H1875) — to seek, to require; “the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee”, Deuteronomy 23:21.

Hebrew nadar (H5087) — to vow; “Vow, and pay unto the LORD your God”, Psalm 76:11.

Usage

"“defer not to pay it” (Ecc 5:4) — a vow is a debt."

"“Better is it that thou shouldest not vow” (Ecc 5:5) — the safer counsel."

"“the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee” (Deu 23:21) — no dispensation available."
